extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, regulatory practitioners, and informed public interested in rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical commentary on the legal and procedural stakes of notice-and-comment rulemaking in light of recent Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Loper Bright, West Virginia v. EPA) and a presidential memorandum directing repeal of regulations. Discusses how precedent, doctrines, and procedures interact to constrain or enable regulatory change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with APA Section 553 (notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act requires agencies to publish notices of proposed rulemakings and to elicit public feedback; the presidential memorandum would have agencies 'finalize rules' rescinding regulations 'without notice and comment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece treats notice-and-comment as a baseline procedural requirement for rulemaking and rescission: bypassing Section 553 (no publication of proposed rules, no public feedback) departs from ordinary APA process and is framed as legally and democratically significant. Example/anti-pattern: finalizing rescissions without publishing proposed rulemakings or soliciting public comment (as urged by the memorandum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loper Bright's limitation on Chevron deference / judicial review of agency interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright overturned Chevron and framed statutory interpretation as primarily the courts' responsibility, urging judges to 'exercise stringent review of agency decisions' to constrain agencies' interpretive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for rulemaking: agencies can no longer rely on Chevron deference for statutory interpretation; courts will more actively scrutinize agency interpretations. The essay warns that this shift, while intended to limit agency power, may have unpredictable downstream effects (including being invoked to justify executive actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine requires clear congressional authorization for major issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine (as in West Virginia v. EPA) demands a clear congressional delegation of authority on major issues, limiting agency action on matters of great political or economic significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an offshoot of nondelegation concerns: the doctrine is 'not so much ... a way of preventing Congress from giving away too much power as a way to prevent Presidents from snatching powers they were not given.' Practically, agencies must point to an unmistakable statutory grant when acting on major questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural safeguards function as a check on executive/agency power
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment and similar procedural constraints operate as important checks in the 'administrative governance game'; abandoning them risks atrophy of procedural constraints on agency rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that removing procedural safeguards (e.g., by finalizing rescissions without public process) could, paradoxically, expand executive influence over regulation over time. Evaluation of regulatory actions should therefore consider whether procedural protections were observed and whether their erosion will change institutional balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper role and invocation of judicial precedent in administrative action
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking Loper Bright and the major questions doctrine to justify sweeping regulatory rescission without normal procedures is a problematic use of precedent: the Court's rhetoric aimed to constrain agencies, yet is being cited to empower executive-initiated rescission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: precedents should not be used as justificatory cover to bypass ordinary procedures; commentators and decisionmakers should be cautious about leveraging case law in ways that undermine procedural norms. Example: the memorandum listing Loper Bright at the top of cases justifying bypassing notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and public input as necessary for legitimate rescission of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescinding regulations should involve 'deliberate care that took into account public input'; large-scale rescissions carried out without such deliberation could amount to improper uses of presidential power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of repeal efforts should ask whether agencies engaged in careful, public-facing processes rather than abrupt, wholesale rescissions. Anti-pattern: characterizing agency determinations that regulations are 'on their face unlawful' as justification for immediate final rescission absent public process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate institutional and political countermoves when altering rulemaking norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant departures from notice-and-comment may 'set off countermoves by any number of other players in the administrative governance game' (courts, Congress, state actors, stakeholders) that could rein in or alter the effects of executive actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for policymakers and analysts: consider likely legal and political responses to procedural bypasses (litigation, congressional action, stakeholder mobilization) when assessing the viability and durability of regulatory changes; regulatory strategy should account for these dynamics.
